query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled short dwell at peak synthesis temperature enables limited atomic diffusion that drives a disorder-to-order phase transition without triggering particle agglomeration or phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: Noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles (with >5 elements) synthesized via rapid Joule heating producing a disordered solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled thermal dwell (e.g., extending heating at ~1100 K for ≈5 min) after initial rapid heating before rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Maintain synthesis temperature around 1100 K, ensuring dwell time is long enough for moderate atomic diffusion but short enough to prevent particle growth, and stay below the decomposition temperature of the metal salts.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced atomic rearrangement at the nanoscale enabling transition from random disordered atomic distribution to an ordered single-phase structure (e.g., L10 intermetallic ordering).
generation.mechanism: The dwell period allows overcoming kinetic constraints by permitting limited diffusion that lowers the formation enthalpy (via spin–orbit coupling and hybridization) driving a thermodynamically favored disorder-to-order transition while rapid quenching preserves the structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles exhibit improved crystallographic order (single-phase solid solution or ordered phase) with uniform morphology and little to no elemental segregation relative to a baseline that omits the dwell.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with only rapid heating and immediate quenching, which tend to display phase separation, uncontrolled morphology or elemental segregation.
generation.boundary: Applicable for compositions composed of >5 noble metal elements; peak temperature must remain around 1100 K and dwell time should be limited (∼5 min) to avoid unwanted grain growth.
generation.uncertainty: The precise dwell duration and its interplay with specific elemental diffusivities might vary with the precursor and substrate, introducing moderate uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of HEA nanoparticles under identical conditions except one includes the controlled dwell at ~1100 K for 5 min and the other is quenched immediately after rapid heating. Compare nanoparticle phase, morphology, and elemental distribution.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess phase ordering
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) for elemental mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of the dwell period does not produce a statistically significant improvement in phase purity, atomic ordering, or results in increased particle growth compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, we demonstrate the synthesis of nanoscale MPEIs (4 to 5 nm) that contain up to eight different elements without particle growth or phase separation via a unique multi-elemental disorder-to-order (HEA to MPEI) phase transition strategy (Fig. 1A). Specifically, we first rapidly Joule-heated metal salt precursors on the carbon substrate [x-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy characterization in fig. S2] at ~1100 K for 55 ms to produce disordered solid-solution HEA nanoparticles as the starting material (). We then use the precise heating control made possible by this Joule-heating approach (in which the reaction temperature is controlled by an electric current) to reheat the HEA nanoparticles for just 5 min at ~1100 K to promote atomic rearrangement to a more thermodynamically stable MPEI configuration (i.e., a disorder-to-order transition), followed by rapid cooling to lock the final ordered structure in place. The resulting MPEI nanoparticles feature an intermetallic structure that has two sublattices (A1B1) (fig. S3a). Taking the octonary (Pt0.8Pd0.1Au0.1)(Fe0.6Co0.1Ni0.1Cu0.1Sn0.1) L10 MPEI that we synthesized as an example, high-angle annular dark

To synthesize the MPEI nanoparticles, we preloaded a carbon substrate with desired metal salt precursor combinations/ratios and Joule-heated (fig. S5) the materials with precise control of the temperature and heating/cooling rates by tuning the power applied to the substrate (fig. S6). The temperature profile and structural evolution of nanoparticles over time are illustrated in Fig. 2A. We first synthesize solid-solution (HEA) nanoparticles () by heating the metal precursors for tens of milliseconds at ~1100 K. This is a critical step for mixing the different elements without phase separation. A disorder-to-order phase transition is then achieved by rapidly reheating the materials to ~1100 K for an additional ~5 min—a limited amount of time that is sufficient to complete the desired transition from the disordered HEA structure to the ordered, single-phase MPEI configuration while simultaneously avoiding nanoparticle growth/agglomeration. Last, the single-phase MPEI structure and small particle size (~5 nm) is preserved by rapidly cooling the materials (~104 K/s).

In summary, we report the first synthesis of MPEI nanoparticles with up to eight constituent elements through a unique disorder-to-order phase transition. This transition is achieved by starting with disordered, solid-solution HEA nanoparticles that are Joule-heated for a short period of time (~5 min) followed by rapid cooling (~104 K/s). The HEA starting materials synthesized through a rapid thermal shock (tens of milliseconds heating) enables the mixing of the diverse elements, regardless of their thermodynamic miscibility. The subsequent ~5 min of heating is then critical to achieve the disorder-to-order transition that converts the HEA nanoparticles into MPEI nanoparticles, which is driven by thermodynamic stability. In addition, the limited heating time and the ensuing rapid temperature quenching prevent the MPEI nanoparticles from excessive growth and agglomeration. This unique approach not only produces stable MPEIs at the nanoscale but also can enable previously unidentified MPEI compositions (e.g., PtPdAuFeCoNiCuSn) that have never been achieved by traditional methods because of the inherent immiscibility of the elements. papers.title: Multi-principal elemental intermetallic nanoparticles synthesized via a disorder-to-order transition.
papers.system: Noble metal–based multi-principal (HEA/MPEI) nanoparticles (e.g., PtPdAuFeCoNiCuSn) synthesized from metal salt precursors on carbon substrates
papers.approach: Rapid Joule heating in two stages – first a tens-of-milliseconds heating at ~1100 K to form a disordered solid-solution HEA nanoparticle, then a short (~5 min) controlled reheat at the same temperature to drive a disorder-to-order phase transition, followed by rapid quenching (~10^4 K/s)
papers.findings: The two-step thermal treatment promotes atomic rearrangement from a random disordered structure into a stable L10 intermetallic (MPEI) configuration while limiting particle growth/agglomeration and avoiding phase separation even in systems of up to eight elements.
papers.mechanism: A controlled thermal pulse allows limited atomic diffusion such that thermodynamic driving forces (including favorable enthalpy decrease from spin‐orbit coupling and metal hybridization) overcome kinetic constraints, fostering a disorder-to-order transition while rapid quenching “locks in” the target single-phase structure.

papers.title: Continuous synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles by in-flight alloying of elemental metals.
papers.system: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles prepared from mixtures of elemental metal powders via a high-temperature plasma jet (e.g., CrFeCoNiMo system)
papers.approach: Ultrafast one-step method using a thermal plasma jet; rapid heating (>5000 K) produces an atomized, multicomponent vapor with subsequent ultrahigh cooling rates (10^3–10^6 K/s). Reactor geometry and plasma gas choice (e.g., H2, He) are adjusted to maximize turbulent mixing and to align the nucleation of different elements.
papers.findings: While rapid heating enables near simultaneous vaporization, the intrinsic differences such as saturation vapor pressures lead to differing nucleation temperatures among elements. Without exact control, elements with low saturation pressures may nucleate first, resulting in elemental segregation or phase separation.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between the high cooling rate, turbulence-induced mixing, and the element-specific nucleation kinetics determines whether a homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution is achieved or whether phase separation occurs owing to sequential nucleation.

papers.title: The more the better: on the formation of single-phase high entropy alloy nanoparticles as catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction.
papers.system: Noble metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles prepared from five-metal single-source precursors (e.g., Pt, Ir, Rh, Os, Ru)
papers.approach: Low-temperature thermolysis of a crystalline single-source precursor under a reductive gas flow, leading to stepwise reduction of metal precursors with limited atomic mobility
papers.findings: Despite a sequential reduction from the precursor, a single-phase HEA forms more readily in five-element systems compared to bimetallic mixtures due to the reduced concentration of any individual element, which hinders local segregation and ordering that would promote phase separation.
papers.mechanism: A kinetic model based on restricted atomic mobility shows that dilution of each element reduces the probability for strongly ordering pairs to segregate, favoring random atomic incorporation. Stochastic principles during nanoparticle formation drive the system toward a homogeneous solid solution.

papers.title: Kinetically Limited Phase Formation of Pt-Ir Based Compositionally Complex Thin Films.
papers.system: Pt-based noble metal thin films containing multiple constituents (e.g., Pt-Ir-Cu-AuX, where X = Ag or Pd)
papers.approach: Physical vapor deposition with control over substrate temperature and deposition kinetics, comparing films where activation energy barriers for surface diffusion are altered by substituting elements (e.g., Ag versus Pd)
papers.findings: Films with higher activation energy barriers (e.g., with Pd) exhibit kinetically trapped metastable single-phase solid solutions, whereas reducing the barrier by substituting Ag increases atomic mobility and leads to phase separation into multiple fcc phases.
papers.mechanism: The phase formation is governed by a balance between thermodynamic driving forces (mixing enthalpy) and the kinetics of atomic surface diffusion. Enhanced kinetic barriers inhibit atomic rearrangement into thermodynamically favored segregated phases under rapid processing conditions.

established: Rapid heating and cooling can kinetically trap a disordered solid solution that can then undergo a controlled disorder-to-order transition under specific thermal conditions.
Element-specific nucleation temperatures (governed by saturation vapor pressures) can lead to phase separation if not properly synchronized.
Restricted atomic mobility due to short heating durations and high cooling rates is key to preventing elemental segregation and uncontrolled particle growth.

approaches_tried.outcome: Successfully produced nanoscale multi-principal intermetallic nanoparticles in a single-phase, ordered configuration by leveraging a disorder-to-order transition.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermal plasma jet synthesis with reactor design modifications and selection of plasma gases
approaches_tried.outcome: Enabled ultrafast synthesis of HEA nanoparticles; however, differences in nucleation temperatures may lead to elemental segregation unless turbulence and residence time are carefully tuned.

approaches_tried.outcome: Promoted formation of single-phase HEA nanoparticles by limiting precursor mobility, though the process is sensitive to kinetic restrictions and the number of constituent elements.

approaches_tried.approach: Controlling elemental surface diffusion in vapor-deposited thin films via compositional tuning (e.g., Ag vs. Pd substitution)
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that higher activation energy barriers can trap metastable single phases, while reduced barriers lead to phase separation.

mechanisms: Interplay of kinetic constraints (limited atomic mobility due to short heating durations and rapid cooling) with thermodynamic driving forces (mixing enthalpy, disorder-to-order transitions)
Element-specific nucleation kinetics dictated by differences in saturation vapor pressures and vapor pressures, leading to co-nucleation challenges

disagreements: Some studies emphasize a thermodynamic explanation (high configurational entropy driving single-phase formation), while others show that kinetic factors such as restricted diffusion and activation energy barriers play a dominant role

open_questions: What are the precise quantitative thresholds (in terms of dwell time, peak temperature, and cooling rate) that separate successful single-phase formation from phase separation in noble metal HEA nanoparticles?
How do subtle differences in elemental properties (e.g., surface diffusion barriers and saturation pressures) interact under rapid processing regimes to dictate crystal-structure selection?
To what extent can controlled kinetic interventions overcome thermodynamic immiscibility in multi-noble metal systems?

directions.assessment: Directly addresses the challenge of limited atomic mobility during rapid heating/cooling by proposing an additional controlled dwell period at peak temperature to enable atomic rearrangement. Supported by evidence on disorder-to-order transitions (PMC8797181::web::003::introduction, PMC8797181::web::005::results) and appears feasible and informative.

Targets the isolated nucleation events due to elemental differences by modulating the heating rate/temperature ramp. This intervention attempts to synchronize nucleation across elements and avoid premature phase separation, as indicated by plasma synthesis studies (PMC10873330::web::003::introduction).

Exploits the statistical advantage of high elemental diversity where lower individual atom concentrations hinder ordered pair segregation. This approach aligns with simulation and kinetic argument evidence (PMC10621632::web::000::abstract, PMC10621632::web::022::simulated_particle_formation_and_influen) and is a known strategy for maintaining single-phase formation.

directions.direction: Reactor gas and thermal environment modification
directions.assessment: Modifies the thermal history via selection of plasma gases or reactor geometry to prolong the liquid droplet phase, enabling adequate mixing and co-nucleation. Evidence from plasma jet synthesis studies (PMC10873330::web::024::effect_of_plasma_gases) supports this intervention as a feasible method to control morphology and phase outcomes.
